1231.event_title: Ono no Komachi's poem of the faded flowers
1231.event: Ono no Komachi, a poet at the Japanese court in the mid-9th century, wrote a famous poem, preserved in the Kokinshū anthology compiled in 905 and later chosen for the Hyakunin Isshu, in which the colour of the flowers has faded while she has let her days slip away, lost in brooding as the long rains fell. Her poems often use fading blossoms as a sign of passing time and fading beauty.
1231.explanation: The poem is one of the best-known expressions in Japanese literature of beauty withering while the heart is absorbed in sorrow.
1231.tie_back: The kural says the wife's eyes have wept away their beauty and now shrink before the flowers they once outshone, and Komachi's poem likewise sets her own fading against faded flowers during days of brooding.
1231._accuracy_note: The pairing of a woman's fading beauty with flowers matches closely, but the poem does not say that the cause is an absent lover.

1232.event_title: Sappho describes the symptoms of longing in fragment 31
1232.event: In the poem now known as fragment 31, the Greek poet Sappho describes watching the person she loves talking with a man and lists what longing does to her body: her tongue breaks, a thin fire runs under her skin, sweat pours down, trembling seizes her and she is greener than grass. The ancient critic Longinus quoted the poem in his treatise On the Sublime as a model description of the symptoms of passion.
1232.explanation: It is the most famous ancient description of love's effect on the body, and it survives because a later critic thought it a perfect example.
1232.tie_back: The kural's eyes, gone sallow and tearful, tell everyone what the heart would hide, and Sappho's poem shows the same thing: a body whose pallor and trembling announce the speaker's longing.
1232._accuracy_note: The body's greenish pallor betraying hidden longing matches the kural's sallow eyes closely, though Sappho's poem is about jealous longing, not a partner's neglect.

1233.event_title: Shah Jahan lives as a mourner after the death of Mumtaz Mahal
1233.event: Mumtaz Mahal, the wife of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, died in 1631. For about two years afterwards the emperor lived as a mourner, going without music, fine clothing and the lavish display of his court.
1233.explanation: The change in the emperor's dress and court life made his private grief visible to everyone around him.
1233.tie_back: The kural's shoulders, once full with the joy of union, grow thin and proclaim the separation to all, and Shah Jahan's plain dress and silent court likewise announced his loss to the whole empire.
1233._accuracy_note: The outward signs of grief announcing a separation to all match, but the separation is a death and the grieving partner is the husband, not the wife.

1234.event_title: Li Qingzhao grows thinner than the yellow flowers
1234.event: Li Qingzhao, the Song dynasty poet, married the official and antiquarian Zhao Mingcheng in 1101, and during his frequent absences she wrote poems of longing for his return. In her song lyric to the tune Drunk under the Shadow of Flowers, set on the Double Ninth festival, the speaker drinks alone by the eastern hedge after dusk and says she has grown thinner than the yellow flowers.
1234.explanation: She is China's most celebrated woman poet, and her lyrics are the classic Chinese picture of a wife wasting away while her husband is gone.
1234.tie_back: The kural says that with her partner gone the wife's shoulders have lost their fullness and her bangles slip, and Li Qingzhao's speaker, alone at dusk, has grown thinner than the flowers.
1234._accuracy_note: Very close: a real wife writing of herself wasting thin during her husband's absence, though the poem speaks of thinness rather than slipping bangles.

1235.event_title: Octavia's loyalty turns Rome against Mark Antony
1235.event: Octavia, sister of Octavian, the future Emperor Augustus, married Mark Antony in 40 BCE to seal the alliance between the two men. After Antony returned to Cleopatra in the East and sent Octavia back to Rome, she went on living in his house as if he were at home, raising her own children and his children by his earlier marriage. Plutarch records that her loyal conduct, without her intending it, damaged Antony, because people hated him for wronging such a woman; he divorced her in 32 BCE.
1235.explanation: Octavia's faithful conduct did more to expose Antony's treatment of her than any accusation could have done.
1235.tie_back: The kural's wasted shoulders and slipping bangles proclaim the cruelty of the one who left, and Octavia's visible, faithful waiting proclaimed Antony's cruelty to all of Rome.
1235._accuracy_note: Strong match: a deserted wife whose evident suffering, not her words, made the public condemn her husband.

1236.event_title: Libbie Custer defends her husband's name for 57 years
1236.event: After George Armstrong Custer died at the Battle of the Little Bighorn in 1876, his widow Elizabeth (Libbie) Bacon Custer learned that President Ulysses S. Grant and senior officers blamed him for the defeat. Widowed at 34 and never remarrying, she spent the rest of her long life protecting his reputation, writing the memoirs Boots and Saddles (1885), Tenting on the Plains (1887) and Following the Guidon (1890). She was buried beside him at the U.S. Military Academy at West Point.
1236.explanation: Her devotion shaped how Americans remembered Custer for half a century, and critics largely held back while she lived.
1236.tie_back: The kural's wife is pained more by hearing her husband called cruel than by her own suffering, and Libbie Custer could not bear to hear her husband blamed and spent decades answering his critics.
1236._accuracy_note: The wife's refusal to let her husband be blamed fits well, but she defended him against charges about a battle, not cruelty to her.

1237.event_title: Kalidasa writes the Meghaduta, the Cloud Messenger
1237.event: Around the 5th century CE the Sanskrit poet Kalidasa wrote the Meghaduta (Cloud Messenger), a lyric love poem of about 115 verses. In it an exiled yaksha, a nature spirit grieving for his beloved on a remote mountain, asks a passing cloud at the start of the monsoon to carry his message to her in the Himalayan city of Alaka, and much of the poem describes the landscapes the cloud will cross.
1237.explanation: The poem became the model for a whole genre of messenger poems in Indian literature.
1237.tie_back: The kural's wife asks her own heart to go to her husband and tell him of her suffering, just as Kalidasa's grieving lover sends a cloud to carry his message to his distant beloved.
1237._accuracy_note: Close in idea, a separated lover sending a messenger across the distance, but the event is the writing of a poem and the messenger is a cloud rather than the heart.

1238.event_title: Nelson Mandela's prison letters to Winnie
1238.place: Robben Island and other prisons, South Africa
1238.event: Nelson Mandela was a sentenced political prisoner from 1962 to 1990, held in four prisons. At first he could write and receive only one 500-word letter every six months, and on Robben Island he was allowed one visitor a year for 30 minutes. In his letters to his wife Winnie he professed his love and gave her moral support in her own struggle.
1238.explanation: The letters show how a separated husband kept his marriage alive through rare, censored words over decades.
1238.tie_back: In this kural the absent husband remembers his wife's tenderness and worries about her, and Mandela, separated from Winnie for decades, poured the same remembering love into his few permitted letters.
1238._accuracy_note: Next-best: it shows a husband far away cherishing his wife, but not the kural's specific memory of her paling at the smallest parting.

1239.event_title: Captain Scott's last letter to his wife Kathleen
1239.event: During the fatal return journey from the South Pole in 1912, Captain Robert Falcon Scott wrote last letters from his tent, including one to his wife Kathleen addressed To my widow. He wrote of the cold, 70 degrees below zero, and asked her to make their son Peter, then about three, interested in natural history if she could. The letter was given to the Scott Polar Research Institute at Cambridge and put on public display in 2007.
1239.explanation: Written as he faced death, the letter shows a husband's last thoughts turning to his wife and child far away.
1239.tie_back: In this kural the husband, far from home, remembers his wife's delicacy and worries how she will bear the separation, and Scott's last letter turns from his own plight to her and their son's future.
1239._accuracy_note: A distant husband's concern for his wife fits, but the kural's tender memory of an embrace interrupted by a breeze has no parallel.

1240.event_title: Rembrandt draws his bride Saskia three days after their betrothal
1240.event: In 1633 Rembrandt van Rijn made a silverpoint drawing on parchment of Saskia and wrote beneath it, in Dutch, that it was a likeness of his wife made when she was 21 years old, on the third day after their betrothal. The drawing is now in the Kupferstichkabinett of the Staatliche Museen zu Berlin.
1240.explanation: It is a rare record of an artist studying the face of the woman he loved at the very start of their life together.
1240.tie_back: The kural's husband remembers every small change in his wife's face, her brow and her eyes, and Rembrandt's drawing shows a lover attending closely to his bride's face.
1240._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it shows a husband's close attention to his wife's face, but nothing of the pallor, grief or separation the kural describes.
